reading.body:
Alaska's AI-related legislation is narrow and early: the two bills explicitly naming AI focus on deepfakes, synthetic media, and election integrity, with a task force resolution added to study the subject rather than regulate it directly.

The pattern across the 13 bills is one of harm mitigation at the edges of AI rather than any structural approach to the technology itself. SB2 pairs AI with cybersecurity and data transfers. SB33 addresses synthetic media liability in the context of elections. HB47 and the social media bills targeting minors are adjacent concerns, involving AI-generated content but framed around child protection. None of the bills address compute, data center siting, energy demand, or the infrastructure that makes AI systems possible.

What the data does not cover is significant. There is no legislation here touching power consumption, grid interconnection, or permitting for large facilities, which are the upstream constraints on AI development. HJR40, titled "Supporting Sustainable Alaska," might be relevant to energy policy, but the data provides only a title, not content. The task force created by HCR3 could eventually produce recommendations on any of these topics, but as of the data available, Alaska's legislative record on AI is limited to content harms and electoral integrity, with the deeper infrastructure questions unaddressed.
